---
title: "List Indexing"
unit: 2
cluster: "Working with Lists"
---

We have seen how to select an element of a list by its index, counting from the
start. Python also lets us count from the end. This makes it easy to select the
last element, or the second-to-last, without knowing the length of the list.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* select an element by counting from the start
* select an element by counting from the end, with negative indexes
* select the last word of a sentence
* tell which indexes are out of range

**Every element of a list has two indexes. Counting from the start, the first
index is `0`. Counting from the end, the last index is `-1`.**

## Counting from the start

This list has five elements:

```{python}
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"]
```

Indexes counted from the start begin at `0`, so the first element has index
`0` and the last element has index `4`:

```{python}
days[0]
```

```{python}
days[4]
```

The last index is always one less than the length of the list. An index can be
any expression that produces an integer, so the last element can be selected
without knowing the length in advance:

```{python}
days[len(days) - 1]
```

This works for a list of any length, but it is long to write and easy to get
wrong.

## Counting from the end

A **negative index** counts from the end of the list. Index `-1` selects the
last element:

```{python}
days[-1]
```

Index `-2` selects the second element from the end:

```{python}
days[-2]
```

Each element of `days` has both kinds of index:

| Element | `"Mon"` | `"Tue"` | `"Wed"` | `"Thu"` | `"Fri"` |
|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|
| Index | `0` | `1` | `2` | `3` | `4` |
| Negative index | `-5` | `-4` | `-3` | `-2` | `-1` |

`days[4]` and `days[-1]` select the same element. `days[-1]` keeps selecting
the last element when the list grows or shrinks; `days[4]` does not.

## The last word of a sentence

The `split()` method returns a list of words, so a negative index selects
words from the end of a sentence:

```{python}
sentence = "this too shall pass"
words = sentence.split()
words[-1]
```

The sentence has four words, but the code does not depend on that. It selects
the last word of any sentence.

The two steps can also be written as one expression. Python calls `split()`
first, then indexes the list it returns:

```{python}
sentence.split()[-1]
```

## Indexes out of range

A list with five elements has indexes `0` to `4` and `-5` to `-1`. Any other
index produces an `IndexError`, from either end:

```python
days[5]
```

```python
days[-6]
```

The last line of the error message is the same for both:

```text
IndexError: list index out of range
```

## Summary

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `days[0]` | selects the first element |
| `days[-1]` | selects the last element |
| `days[-2]` | selects the second element from the end |
| `days[len(days) - 1]` | selects the last element by counting from the start |
| `sentence.split()[-1]` | selects the last word of `sentence` |
| a list of length `n` | has indexes `0` to `n - 1` and `-n` to `-1` |
| any other index | raises `IndexError: list index out of range` |

And the one idea to carry forward: an index can count from either end of a
list. Index `0` is the first element and index `-1` is the last.
